stem: In which order does food pass through these parts of the alimentary canal?

options.content: mouth → stomach → oesophagus → small intestine → large intestine → anus
options.rationale: The oesophagus comes before the stomach.

options.content: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → anus
options.rationale: This is the correct order.

options.content: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → large intestine → small intestine → anus
options.rationale: The small intestine comes before the large intestine.

options.content: mouth → oesophagus → liver → stomach → small intestine → anus
options.rationale: Food never passes through the liver; it is an associated organ.

explanation: Food travels mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine (duodenum, then ileum) → large intestine (colon, then rectum) → anus. The liver, pancreas and gall bladder are associated organs that food does not pass through.
hints: The tube from the mouth to the stomach is the oesophagus.

stem: Which organ **makes** bile?

options.rationale: Liver cells make bile continuously.
The gall bladder stores bile but does not make it.
The pancreas makes pancreatic juice, which contains enzymes.
The stomach makes gastric juice, which contains acid and a protease.

explanation: Bile is made in the liver, stored in the gall bladder and released through the bile duct into the duodenum.
hints: The organ that makes bile is the largest organ in the abdomen.

stem: Match each process with its description.

right.content: Taking food and drink into the body through the mouth
Breaking large insoluble molecules into small soluble molecules
Movement of digested food molecules from the intestine into the blood
Uptake and use of nutrients by body cells
Passing out undigested food as faeces through the anus
Removal of the waste products of metabolism, such as urea

explanation: Ingestion takes food in, digestion breaks it down, absorption moves the products into the blood, assimilation is their use by cells and egestion removes the undigested remains. The unused description is excretion, which removes waste made by cells.
hints: One description belongs to excretion, which is not in the list.

stem: True or false: passing out undigested food as faeces is an example of **excretion**.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not true. Undigested food never entered the body's cells, so removing it is egestion.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. It is egestion; excretion removes waste products made inside cells, such as urea and carbon dioxide.

explanation: Excretion removes waste products of metabolism (made inside cells), such as urea and carbon dioxide. Undigested food in faeces was never absorbed into cells, so passing it out is egestion.
hints: Was the undigested food ever inside the body's cells?

stem: Where are most digested food molecules absorbed into the blood?

options.rationale: Very little is absorbed through the stomach wall; it mainly churns food and starts protein digestion.
The large intestine absorbs mainly water and some mineral ions.
The ileum absorbs nearly all the digested food.
The liver receives absorbed nutrients from the blood; food does not pass through it.

explanation: The small intestine, especially the ileum, absorbs nearly all the digested food (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol) and most of the water. The colon absorbs some water and mineral ions.
hints: Which part of the canal is very long and has a huge surface area?

stem: Name the organ that **stores** bile until it is released into the duodenum.

rejected.feedback: The liver makes bile; it is stored elsewhere.
The urinary bladder stores urine. Bile is stored in the gall bladder.

explanation: Bile made in the liver is stored in the gall bladder, a small sac beneath the liver, and released through the bile duct into the duodenum, especially after a fatty meal.
hints: It is a small sac tucked beneath the liver.

stem: What is the main function of the colon?

options.content: Digesting the last of the protein left in the food
options.rationale: Protein is digested in the stomach and small intestine.
Bile is made by the liver.

options.content: Absorbing most of the glucose from food into the blood
options.rationale: Glucose is absorbed in the small intestine.

options.content: Absorbing water from the undigested remains of food
options.rationale: This turns liquid waste into semi-solid faeces.

explanation: By the time food reaches the colon, the useful molecules have been absorbed. The colon absorbs much of the remaining water (and some mineral ions), so the faeces become semi-solid before they are stored in the rectum.
hints: What happens to the watery remains so that faeces become semi-solid?

stem: An organ releases a juice containing amylase, protease and lipase into the duodenum through a duct, but food never passes through the organ itself. Which organ is it?

options.rationale: Food passes through the stomach, and gastric juice contains a protease but not amylase or lipase.
Pancreatic juice contains all three enzymes and enters the duodenum.
The gall bladder releases bile, which contains no enzymes.
Salivary glands release saliva into the mouth, and it contains amylase only.

explanation: The pancreas is an associated organ lying below the stomach. Its juice contains amylase, protease (trypsin) and lipase and flows along the pancreatic duct into the duodenum.
hints: Which associated organ makes enzymes for all three main food types?

stem: Complete the sentences about the alimentary canal.

payload.template: The muscular tube that carries food from the mouth to the stomach is the {{blank:oes}}. The first part of the small intestine, which receives bile and pancreatic juice, is the {{blank:duo}}. Faeces are stored in the {{blank:rec}} before they are egested.

explanation: The oesophagus (gullet) carries food to the stomach. The duodenum is the first part of the small intestine, where bile and pancreatic juice arrive. The rectum stores faeces until they pass out through the anus.
hints: The trachea carries air, not food.

stem: During peristalsis, what happens in the wall of the oesophagus just **behind** a ball of food?

options.content: Circular muscles contract and longitudinal ones relax, squeezing food on.
options.rationale: Narrowing behind the food pushes it along.

options.content: The circular muscles relax and the longitudinal muscles contract, so the tube widens.
options.rationale: This happens in front of the food, to make room for it.

options.content: Both layers of muscle relax, so gravity pulls the food down.
options.rationale: Peristalsis does not depend on gravity; we can swallow lying down.

options.content: Enzymes in the wall digest the food, making it move.
options.rationale: Digestion does not move food; muscles do.

explanation: Behind the food the circular muscles contract, narrowing the tube and pushing the food forward. In front of it the circular muscles relax and the longitudinal muscles contract, widening the tube. These waves pass all along the canal.
hints: To squeeze toothpaste out of a tube, which part of the tube do you narrow?

stem: True or false: on its way to the small intestine, food passes through the liver.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not true. The liver is an associated organ; food stays inside the alimentary canal.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. Food passes from the stomach straight into the duodenum. The liver adds bile through a duct.

explanation: Food travels only along the alimentary canal. The liver is an associated organ: it makes bile, which reaches the duodenum through the bile duct, and later receives absorbed nutrients in the blood.
hints: Is the liver part of the tube?

stem: Which substance leaves the body by **egestion** rather than by excretion?

options.rationale: Urea is made in the liver from excess amino acids, so removing it is excretion.

options.content: Carbon dioxide in the air breathed out
options.rationale: Carbon dioxide is made by respiration in cells, so removing it is excretion.
Cellulose was never digested or absorbed, so passing it out is egestion.
Salts removed in sweat have been in the blood and tissues, so this is excretion.

explanation: Egestion removes material that was never absorbed into the body, such as cellulose fibre. Urea, carbon dioxide and excess salts have been inside the body's cells or blood and are removed by excretion.
hints: Which substance was never absorbed into the blood?

stem: On a front-view diagram of the human digestive system, organ X is the largest organ in the abdomen. It lies just below the diaphragm on the person's right side and partly covers the stomach. A small sac is tucked beneath it. What is organ X?

options.rationale: The pancreas is a flattened gland below and behind the stomach, much smaller than X.
X partly covers the stomach, so it cannot be the stomach.
The colon frames the coils of the small intestine in the lower abdomen.
The liver is the largest organ in the abdomen, under the diaphragm on the right, with the gall bladder beneath it.

explanation: The liver is the largest internal organ. It lies under the diaphragm on the body's right side, partly over the stomach, and the gall bladder (the small sac) sits beneath it.
hints: Which organ has the gall bladder beneath it?

stem: Which statement describes the role of the stomach?

options.content: It absorbs most of the digested food into the blood.
options.rationale: Most absorption happens in the small intestine.

options.content: Its muscular walls churn food with acid and a protease.
options.rationale: The stomach mixes food, kills microorganisms and starts protein digestion.

options.content: It makes bile, which is stored in the gall bladder.
options.rationale: Bile is made by the liver.

options.content: It absorbs water to form the semi-solid faeces.
options.rationale: That is the role of the colon.

explanation: The stomach stores food for a few hours, churns it (mechanical digestion) and mixes it with gastric juice. The hydrochloric acid kills many microorganisms and the protease starts digesting protein.
hints: Think about the stomach's muscular walls and the juice it makes.

stem: State the term for the uptake of absorbed nutrients by body cells and their use to build or run the cells.

rejected.feedback: Absorption is the movement into the blood; the use by cells is assimilation.
Digestion breaks food down before it is absorbed.
Ingestion is taking food into the mouth.

explanation: Assimilation follows absorption: cells take up nutrients and use them, for example to make proteins from amino acids or to store glucose as glycogen.
hints: It comes after absorption in the sequence of five processes.

stem:
A student describes the positions of some labelled organs on a front-view diagram of the digestive system.

| Label | Description on the diagram |
| --- | --- |
| A | A narrow tube running down the centre of the chest, behind the windpipe |
| B | A J-shaped muscular bag on the person's left side, just below the diaphragm |
| C | The largest organ in the abdomen, on the person's right side, just below the diaphragm |
| D | A small sac tucked beneath C |
| E | A flattened gland lying below and behind B, in the curve of the duodenum |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Match each label with the organ it shows.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which **two** labels show the organ that **stores** bile and the organ that **makes** pancreatic juice?

options.rationale: A and B are the oesophagus and the stomach, which are part of the canal; neither stores bile or makes pancreatic juice.
D, the gall bladder, stores bile, and E, the pancreas, makes pancreatic juice; both are released into the duodenum through ducts.
C, the liver, makes bile but does not store it, and B, the stomach, makes gastric juice, not pancreatic juice.
E, the pancreas, is right, but A is the oesophagus, which only carries food to the stomach.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Some people have their gall bladder removed. Bile then trickles from the liver into the duodenum all the time, in small amounts. Suggest why these people may find large, fatty meals harder to digest.

points.description: No store of bile, so a large amount cannot be released when fatty food arrives
Less bile to emulsify the fat / smaller surface area for lipase, so fat is digested more slowly

parts.explanation: Without a gall bladder there is no store of bile, so a large amount cannot be released when a fatty meal reaches the duodenum. Less fat is emulsified, so there is a smaller surface area for lipase and the fat is digested more slowly.

explanation: A is the oesophagus, B the stomach, C the liver, D the gall bladder and E the pancreas. The gall bladder and pancreas both release their juices into the duodenum. Without the gall bladder's store, less bile is available for a large fatty meal, so less fat is emulsified and digestion of fat is slower.
hints: The gall bladder sits beneath the liver.
For (c), think about what bile does to fat droplets.

stem: Rudo eats a meal of rice and beans.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Where does the chemical digestion of the starch in the rice **begin**?

options.rationale: Salivary amylase begins starch digestion while the food is chewed.
Starch digestion has already started before food reaches the stomach.
Pancreatic amylase continues starch digestion here, but it does not begin here.
Digestion is finished before food reaches the colon.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Where does the chemical digestion of the protein in the beans **begin**?

options.rationale: Saliva contains amylase but no protease.
Protein digestion is completed here, but it began earlier.
The oesophagus carries food; it does not secrete enzymes.
Gastric juice contains a protease that starts protein digestion.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Name the process by which the digested food molecules pass from the small intestine into the blood.

rejected.feedback: Assimilation is the use of nutrients by cells after absorption.
Digestion breaks food down; absorption moves it into the blood.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: The beans contain a lot of fibre. Describe what happens to this fibre in the large intestine.

points.description: It is not digested (humans cannot digest cellulose) / it adds bulk
Water is absorbed from it in the colon and it is stored in the rectum, then egested through the anus as faeces

parts.explanation: The fibre is not digested, so it reaches the large intestine. The colon absorbs water from it, and it forms bulky faeces that are stored in the rectum and egested through the anus.

explanation: Starch digestion begins in the mouth (salivary amylase); protein digestion begins in the stomach (protease in gastric juice). The digested products are absorbed in the small intestine. Fibre is not digested: the colon absorbs water from it and it leaves as faeces.
hints: Which enzyme is in saliva, and which is in gastric juice?

stem: Describe what happens to a meal as it passes through the alimentary canal, from ingestion to egestion. Name the organs involved. [6]

points.description: Ingestion through the mouth; teeth chew food into smaller pieces (mechanical digestion)
Saliva (from salivary glands) moistens food and its amylase starts starch digestion
Food is swallowed and carried down the oesophagus (by peristalsis)
Stomach churns food; acid kills microorganisms; protease starts protein digestion
Duodenum receives bile (liver / gall bladder) and pancreatic juice; digestion continues
Ileum completes digestion and absorbs digested food (and most water) into the blood
Colon absorbs water from undigested remains; rectum stores faeces; egestion through the anus

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Food is ingested through the mouth, where the teeth chew it into smaller pieces and saliva from the salivary glands moistens it; salivary amylase begins to digest starch. Each swallowed ball of food passes down the oesophagus by peristalsis to the stomach. The stomach churns the food with gastric juice: hydrochloric acid kills microorganisms and a protease begins protein digestion. In the duodenum, bile from the liver (stored in the gall bladder) and pancreatic juice from the pancreas are added and digestion continues. The ileum completes digestion and absorbs the small soluble molecules and most of the water into the blood. In the colon more water is absorbed from the undigested remains, which are stored as faeces in the rectum and egested through the anus.

explanation: A full answer follows the meal through each organ in order and names one process or juice at each stage, ending with egestion.
hints: Work through the organs in order and say one thing that happens in each.

stem: Which row correctly shows where each process takes place?

options.content: Ingestion: stomach; absorption: small intestine; egestion: anus
options.rationale: Food is ingested through the mouth.

options.content: Ingestion: mouth; absorption: stomach; egestion: anus
options.rationale: Most absorption happens in the small intestine.

options.content: Ingestion: mouth; absorption: small intestine; egestion: anus
options.rationale: All three are correct.

options.content: Ingestion: mouth; absorption: small intestine; egestion: kidneys
options.rationale: The kidneys excrete urine; faeces are egested through the anus.

explanation: Food is ingested through the mouth, digested food is absorbed mainly in the small intestine, and undigested food is egested through the anus.
hints: Check each place in turn; only one row is right for all three.

stem: Which of these is an associated organ of digestion and **not** part of the alimentary canal?

options.rationale: The stomach is part of the alimentary canal.
The oesophagus is part of the alimentary canal.
The colon is part of the large intestine, so it is part of the canal.
The pancreas releases juice into the duodenum, but food does not pass through it.

explanation: The alimentary canal is the tube that food passes through. The salivary glands, liver, gall bladder and pancreas are associated organs that add juices to it.
hints: Food does not pass through an associated organ.

stem: True or false: the small intestine is longer than the large intestine.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct. The small intestine is several metres long; the large intestine is wider but much shorter.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. 'Small' refers to its narrow width: the small intestine is several metres long, much longer than the large intestine.

explanation: The names refer to width, not length. The small intestine is narrow but several metres long, giving time and surface area for digestion and absorption. The large intestine is wider but much shorter.

stem: True or false: peristalsis depends on gravity, so food cannot move along the oesophagus when a person is lying down.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not true. Peristalsis is caused by muscle contractions, so it works in any position.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. Waves of muscle contraction push the food, so we can swallow lying down (and astronauts can swallow in space).

explanation: Peristalsis is a wave of contraction of the circular and longitudinal muscles in the wall of the canal. It pushes food along whatever the position of the body.
hints: What actually pushes the food along?

stem: After an injury, a patient had most of the ileum removed by surgery. Suggest and explain **two** problems the patient is likely to have with digestion and nutrition. [4]

points.description: Less digested food (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids) is absorbed
because the length / surface area of the small intestine available for absorption is much smaller (and food spends less time there)
So the patient may lose body mass / become malnourished / lack vitamins and mineral ions
More water (and undigested food) reaches the colon
so the faeces are watery / the patient has diarrhoea and may become dehydrated

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The ileum is where most digested food is absorbed. With most of it removed, the surface area and the time available for absorption are much smaller, so less glucose, amino acids, fats, vitamins and mineral ions reach the blood; the patient may lose mass and become malnourished. The ileum also absorbs most of the water, so much more water reaches the colon than it can absorb, giving watery faeces (diarrhoea) and a risk of dehydration.

explanation: The ileum completes digestion and absorbs nearly all the digested food and most of the water, so losing most of it reduces absorption of nutrients and water.
hints: What are the two main jobs of the ileum?
Think about both nutrients and water.

stem: Volunteers swallowed a harmless coloured marker with a meal, and the time until it first appeared in their faeces was recorded. Group 1 ate a high-fibre diet (whole-grain maize meal, beans and vegetables); group 2 ate a low-fibre diet. The mean time was 30 hours for group 1 and 55 hours for group 2. (The data are hypothetical.)

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage increase in the time taken for group 2 compared with group 1. Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why food passed through the gut more quickly in group 1.

points.description: Fibre is not digested, so it adds bulk to the food
The muscles of the gut wall push bulky food along more easily / faster (peristalsis)

parts.explanation: Fibre is not digested, so it adds bulk to the food in the gut. The muscles of the gut wall can push bulky food along more easily, so it moves through faster.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: In which part of the alimentary canal is water absorbed from the undigested remains of food, making the faeces semi-solid?

options.rationale: Very little is absorbed in the stomach.
The oesophagus only carries food to the stomach.
The colon absorbs water from the undigested remains.
The duodenum receives bile and pancreatic juice; the remaining water is absorbed later.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: The faeces of group 2 were harder and drier. Use your answer to (c) to suggest why.

points.description: The undigested remains stayed in the colon for longer
so more water was absorbed from them

parts.explanation: Food moved more slowly in group 2, so the remains spent longer in the colon and more water was absorbed from them, leaving hard, dry faeces (constipation).

explanation: Increase $= 55 - 30 = 25$ hours, so $\dfrac{25}{30} \times 100 = 83.3\%$. Undigested fibre adds bulk that the gut muscles push along quickly. Slow-moving remains spend longer in the colon, which absorbs more water, so the faeces become hard and dry.
hints: Percentage increase compares the increase with the smaller (original) value.
What does fibre give the gut muscles to push against?
